leaf: Containers, Docker, Kubernetes orchestration, Infrastructure as Code and DevOps
verbatim_syllabus: Cloud Architecture and Distributed Systems: Evolution of Distributed, Edge and Cloud Computing; NIST Cloud Architecture; Cloud Deployment and Service Models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS, Serverless); Cloud-native Architecture, Microservices, Service Mesh, Elasticity, High Availability, Load Balancing, and Sustainable Cloud Computing. Virtualization and Cloud Infrastructure: Virtual Machines, Hypervisors, Full and Para Virtualization; CPU, Storage, and Network Virtualization; Containers, Docker Architecture, Kubernetes orchestration, Resource Management, Infrastructure as Code using Terraform and Ansible, CI/CD Pipelines, and DevOps Practices. Cloud Storage, Compute, Networking, Managed Databases, Serverless Computing, Monitoring and Observability, OpenStack, Hybrid and Multi-cloud Management, and AI/ML Infrastructure. Cloud Security and Governance: Shared Responsibility Model, IAM, MFA, Zero Trust Security, Encryption, Backup and Disaster Recovery, Container and Kubernetes Security, DevSecOps, API Security, Virtualization Attacks, FinOps, and Service Level Agreements (SLAs).

existing_stems.q: A container in a Kubernetes Pod declares a memory request of 256Mi and a memory limit of 512Mi. Which statement about how those two values are used is correct?
existing_stems.ans_text: The scheduler places the Pod against the 256Mi request, and the container is terminated if its usage exceeds 512Mi

existing_stems.q: Terraform and Ansible are both used to manage infrastructure as code. Which description of the usual division of labour between them is accurate?
existing_stems.ans_text: Terraform declares desired infrastructure and reconciles it against recorded state to create, change or destroy resources, while Ansible is primarily agentless configuration management that runs tasks over SSH

existing_stems.q: Linux containers rest on two distinct kernel mechanisms. Which one caps how much CPU time and memory a container may consume, as opposed to controlling what it can see?
